summary:
Article 347-1 of the penal code in Cameroon criminalises both male and female same-sex sexual activity and carries up to five years' imprisonment. The first penal code enacted in 1965 did not criminalise consensual same-sex acts. An ordinance issued in September 1972 by President Ahmadou Ahidjo introduced Article 347bis, now numbered 347-1. The 2016 penal code explicitly outlawed same-sex relations. Under the earlier provision sentences ran between six months and five years.

In Douala on 8 February 2021, two transgender women, Shakiro and Patricia, were arrested in a restaurant for wearing women's clothing. Shakiro, born 29 July 1997 in Douala, had built a Facebook and YouTube following discussing trans life. Both women were convicted of attempted homosexuality, public indecency and failing to carry identification. Each received five years' imprisonment plus a fine of 200,000 CFA francs ($370), the maximum statutory term. They had been detained since February 2021 and spent five months in prison before a judge ordered release pending appeal. An appeal was filed. Defence lawyers Alice Nkom and Richard Tamfu described the verdict as a political decision with no proof of acts. Shakiro subsequently fled Cameroon to claim asylum abroad.

Gender presentation alone has supported convictions in earlier cases. In November 2011 Jonas Kimie and Franky Ndome were sentenced to five years after arrest outside a nightclub. The trial judge treated manner of speech, wearing women's clothing and ordering a cream-based liquor as sufficient evidence of homosexuality. No sexual act was observed. An appeals court acquitted both men on 9 January 2013.

Enforcement extends beyond presentation cases. In 2011 at least a dozen men were detained under Section 347. Jean-Claude Roger Mbede was sentenced to three years at Kondengui Central Prison for sending SMS messages to a male acquaintance. On 24 November 2011 three young men were sentenced to five years for oral sex in a parked car. In May 2005 eleven men were arrested at a nightclub on suspicion of sodomy. Authorities threatened medical examinations to prove activity. The men remained detained into February 2006, with trials scheduled for March 2006 and release in April 2006.

Human Rights Watch documented an uptick of violence in 2022. Since 9 March of that year security forces arbitrarily arrested at least six people and detained eleven people, all victims of group attacks, for alleged consensual same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity. Gendarmes beat two detainees. The organisation found that the criminalisation law enables abuse by civilians and security forces without consequence, a finding attributed to senior researcher Ilaria Allegrozzi. Beatings of gay and trans people in public are reported as common.

Law No. 2010/012 of 21 December 2010 on Cybersecurity and Cybercrime further punishes same-sex propositioning online. Article 83(1) punishes sexual propositions to a person of the same sex through electronic communications with one to two years' imprisonment and a fine of 500,000 to 1,000,000 CFA francs, or one of those penalties. Article 83(2) doubles the penalty where intercourse followed.

Failure to carry identification was charged alongside the anti-homosexuality counts against Shakiro and Patricia. Prison conditions pose an additional risk. Prisoners accused of homosexuality describe the main prison in Douala as hell.
tangentialFactors:
Cameroon is counted among 31 countries on the African continent that criminalise same-sex conduct. A 2020 assessment described Cameroon as prosecuting consensual same-sex conduct more aggressively than almost any country in the world. Reporting places it among the states in Africa with the highest prosecution rates.

Official statements have minimised the scope of prosecution. In July 2010, after the United Kingdom granted a gay Cameroonian man the right to claim asylum, Minister of Communication Issa Tchiroma Bakary argued that homosexuals are not prosecuted for private activities. President Paul Biya publicly urged respect for privacy while prosecutions of people accused of homosexual activity continued.

On 30 June 2024 Brenda Biya, the daughter of President Biya, came out as a lesbian on Instagram. The announcement drew national backlash and expressions of hope among LGBTQ Cameroonians.
localsOnly:
Alternatives-Cameroon, an LGBTQ organization, was forced to shut down after a police raid, removing a service base inside the country. Few lawyers are willing to defend people accused in homosexuality cases.

The United States Department of State 2010 human rights report for Cameroon noted harassment and extortion of gays and lesbians by law enforcement. False allegations are used to harass or extort.

In 2006 tabloids published the names of at least 50 prominent people claimed to be homosexual, increasing circulation. The state communication council criticised the publications for invasion of privacy.
